messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmad is a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man married to his high school sweetheart. He works as a paramedic and has dedicated much of his life to saving others. However, a traumatic event involving the death of one of his young patients has left him struggling with severe PTSD symptoms. The trauma occurred on a particularly busy shift when Ahmad was dispatched to assist in an accident that involved several pedestrians injured by a hit-and-run driver. Among those critically injured was a small child who succumbed to their injuries despite Ahmad’s best efforts. This event, vividly etched in his memory, has triggered profound distress and flashbacks whenever he encounters visible injuries or the antiseptic smell of hospitals. Since the incident, Ahmad has found himself avoiding work as much as possible due to these triggers. When forced to go on duty, he becomes overwhelmed by memories of that day, which feel completely real across all his senses. These intense recollections not only bring back the same terror he experienced then but also leave him feeling permanently changed for the worse and convinced that he failed in his duty to protect others. The weight of these negative appraisals has led Ahmad to suppress thoughts about the trauma by immersing himself in work or other tasks, often working excessive hours. This overworking is a desperate attempt to keep his mind occupied and avoid confronting the distressing memories, but it has only compounded his difficulties. His concentration at work has significantly deteriorated, making him more prone to startling easily when touched unexpectedly. He also consistently chooses seats based on how safe or protected he feels. One recent evening, Ahmad was called to a scene where another child had been injured in an accident. As soon as he arrived and saw the visible injuries of the victim, his mind immediately flooded with the memory of that fateful day. The antiseptic smell of the hospital only amplified these sensations, sending him into a state of panic and causing him to react with alarm when a colleague tried to console him. This incident was particularly traumatic because it reminded him not only of his perceived failure but also reinforced his belief that he could no longer rely on himself in critical situations. As a result, Ahmad has become increasingly isolated from his colleagues at work and often avoids going to the hospital altogether. When he does go, he finds himself struggling with concentration and becomes hyper-vigilant about potential triggers. Despite these efforts, the memories continue to surface unpredictably, especially when he is in environments reminiscent of the traumatic event, such as a bustling emergency room or an accident scene. These intrusive recollections lead him to feel even more anxious and further reinforce his negative appraisals that he has permanently changed for the worse and cannot rely on himself. The accumulation of these symptoms and experiences has significantly impacted Ahmad’s personal life as well. He is now distant from his wife, often cancelling plans or becoming irritable due to the overwhelming distress triggered by memories and work-related situations. His increasing isolation and inability to cope with daily triggers have finally pushed him to seek help. Ahmad is most afraid that he will never be able to return to his former self, believing deeply that the trauma has left an indelible mark on him. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain control over his life, manage his symptoms effectively, and find a sense of peace amidst the constant reminders of the traumatic event. In summary, Ahmad’s PTSD is characterized by a complex interplay between his triggers, maladaptive strategies, perceptions of threat, memory intrusions, and negative appraisals. Each component feeds into and exacerbates the others, creating a self-perpetuating cycle that has significantly impacted both his professional life as a paramedic and his personal relationships.
